subChunks.title: Language Acquisition & the Cognitive Architecture of Language
subChunks.hookHtml: Every typically developing child, regardless of the language spoken around them, regardless of whether anyone explicitly teaches them grammar, regardless of whether they are high or low in general intelligence, masters the basic grammatical structure of their native language by around age 4–5 — achieving a feat of linguistic complexity that no computer system could reliably perform until very recently. How? This question drove one of psychology's most consequential debates. On one side, B.F. Skinner proposed that language acquisition was just conditioning — parents reward correct speech, punish errors, and children learn through reinforcement. On the other, Noam Chomsky published a devastating critique in 1959, arguing that children are exposed to far too little, too impoverished, and too inconsistent linguistic input for conditioning to explain what they achieve — and that they must therefore possess an innate Language Acquisition Device (LAD) preprogrammed with universal grammar. The debate — nature vs. nurture, nativism vs. empiricism — has shaped not just psychology but linguistics, philosophy of mind, and cognitive science.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Structure of Language

Linguists distinguish several levels of language structure:

Phonology   — The sound system: phonemes are the smallest units of sound
              (English has ~44 phonemes). Infants distinguish phonemes from
              birth but lose sensitivity to non-native phonemes by ~10 months.

Morphology  — The structure of words: morphemes are the smallest meaningful
              units. 'Unbreakable' = un- + break + -able (3 morphemes).

Syntax      — The rules governing sentence structure: word order,
              grammatical relations ('The cat chased the mouse' vs.
              'The mouse chased the cat').

Semantics   — Meaning: the relationship between words/sentences and
              the concepts they represent.

Pragmatics  — Language in use: conversational norms, context-appropriate
              language, implication and inference beyond literal meaning.

Language Acquisition: The Nativist Account

Chomsky (1957, 1959) argued that human language is characterised by productivity (the ability to generate infinitely many sentences from a finite set of rules) and displacement (the ability to refer to absent or hypothetical events). These properties are universal across all human languages — the surface forms differ enormously, but deep structural similarities suggest a common underlying Universal Grammar.

The Poverty of the Stimulus argument: children's linguistic input is impoverished — full of false starts, incomplete sentences, performance errors — and they nevertheless acquire complex grammatical rules without explicit instruction. Chomsky argued this is only explicable if children are born with specific innate language knowledge (the LAD) that enables them to 'project' beyond their input.

Evidence for nativism: the Critical Period Hypothesis — children who are not exposed to language during a critical window (approximately birth to puberty) never achieve full native-like language competence. The case of Genie, a child raised in severe isolation until age 13, is often cited: despite intensive language teaching, she never mastered syntax, though her lexical and pragmatic abilities developed substantially.

Language Acquisition: Interactionist and Social-Pragmatic Accounts

Chomsky's nativism has been criticised for underestimating the role of input and social interaction. Usage-based theories (Tomasello, 2003) propose that language acquisition is driven by domain-general cognitive abilities (pattern recognition, analogy-making, joint attention) interacting with rich social input — children learn language the same way they learn everything else, through experience and social scaffolding, not through a language-specific module.

Evidence for the importance of input: Hart and Risley's (1995) landmark study found that by age 3, children from professional families had heard 30 million more words than children from welfare-dependent families — a '30 million word gap'. This linguistic environment difference predicted vocabulary development, reading ability, and later academic achievement. The quality of child-directed speech (motherese/parentese — a simplified, higher-pitched, clearly articulated speech register used by caregivers) also predicts language development.

Milestones of Language Development

0–6 months    Cooing; responds to human voices
6–8 months    Canonical babbling (babababa, dadada)
8–12 months   Comprehension precedes production; joint attention
10–12 months  First words (typically names, actions, social words)
~18 months    Vocabulary spurt (10+ new words/day)
18–24 months  Two-word combinations ('More milk', 'Daddy go')
2–3 years     Telegraphic speech; beginning of grammar
4–5 years     Essentially adult-like grammar in native language

Language and Thought: The Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis

Does the language we speak influence how we think? The strong version (linguistic determinism): language determines thought — without the words, the thoughts are impossible. This is largely rejected: pre-linguistic infants and non-human animals show conceptual reasoning without language; Deaf individuals raised without sign language still show concept formation.

The weak version (linguistic relativity): language influences thought in some domains. Evidence: Winawer et al. (2007) found that Russian speakers, who have distinct lexical terms for light and dark blue (goluboy vs. siniy), were faster at discriminating shades that crossed the Russian lexical boundary than shades within the same lexical category — suggesting language-specific categories influenced perceptual discrimination. Languages differ in spatial reference frames, time metaphors, and colour categories, and these differences predict corresponding differences in non-linguistic cognition — though effect sizes are modest.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen plays a recording of a 2-year-old saying 'goed' (for 'went') and 'feets' (for 'feet'). The room laughs. She points to why this is more significant than it looks.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: These errors — 'goed', 'feets', 'mouses' — are crucial evidence for nativism. The child has never heard an adult say 'goed'. They are applying a generalised past-tense rule — add -ed — to an irregular verb. This is not imitation. This is rule extraction and creative application. That a two-year-old can extract abstract grammatical rules from messy, variable input and apply them productively is exactly what Chomsky was pointing to.

storyBeats.speaker: The 30 million word gap
storyBeats.text: Hart and Risley (1995) recorded natural language interactions in 42 American families over 2.5 years. By age 3, children from high-income professional families had heard an average of 45 million words; children from welfare-dependent families had heard an average of 13 million — a gap of 32 million words. The quality of interaction also differed: professional parents used more affirmatives and more diverse vocabulary; welfare-dependent families used more prohibitions. These environmental differences predicted vocabulary size at age 3 and reading scores at age 9 with remarkable consistency.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, in its strong form, has not withstood empirical scrutiny — your thoughts are not limited to your words. But in its weak form, it survives: language creates cognitive grooves, habitual ways of carving up the world, that make certain distinctions easier and others harder to attend to. Whether your language has separate words for 'light blue' and 'dark blue' affects how quickly you notice the difference between them. Language is not thought, but it's not neutral either.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A developmental psychologist is designing an intervention to improve language development in children aged 18–36 months from low-income families. She is working with a limited budget and needs to decide between two approaches: (A) providing educational tablet apps with vocabulary-building games; and (B) providing training and support for parents on how to talk more to their children during everyday activities (e.g., narrating actions during cooking and shopping).

  1. Based on the research on language development, which approach does the evidence more strongly support? Explain your reasoning.
  2. What specific features of language input does the research suggest are most important for vocabulary development?
  3. What does the '30 million word gap' finding tell us about the relationship between language development and social inequality?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. The evidence more strongly supports Approach B (parent training). Research on language acquisition consistently emphasises the role of child-directed speech and interactive joint attention in vocabulary development — both of which require a responsive human interlocutor, not a screen. Zimmerman et al. (2007) found that television viewing did not improve language development and may have displaced parent-child interaction. More recent research on screen time and language shows that interactive human conversation is substantially more effective than educational media, particularly for children under 2–3 years. Parent training leverages the naturally occurring, contextually embedded interactions (cooking, shopping, bath time) that provide the kind of rich, responsive input that research identifies as the primary driver of language development.

2. Research identifies several features of language input as particularly important. Quantity: more words heard predicts larger vocabulary (Hart & Risley, 1995). Diversity: the variety of different word types and sentence structures in input predicts language breadth. Contingency: responsiveness — parents who respond promptly and appropriately to infant vocalisations — supports language development more than non-contingent input. Child-directed speech (parentese): the simplified, higher-pitched, clearly articulated register adults spontaneously use with infants, which exaggerates phonemic contrasts and helps infants segment the speech stream. Joint attention: following the child's gaze and commenting on the focus of the child's attention facilitates word-object mapping.

3. The '30 million word gap' demonstrates that language development — one of the foundational determinants of subsequent academic achievement and life outcomes — is substantially shaped by social inequality before children even enter formal education. Children from lower-income families arrive at school with smaller vocabularies and less developed grammatical knowledge, not because of any intrinsic difference in cognitive potential, but because the quality and quantity of their early language environment was constrained by the circumstances of poverty (parental time pressures, stress, educational background). This has profound implications for social mobility: inequalities in language experience translate into inequalities in reading, academic achievement, and ultimately employment — making early language intervention one of the highest-return investments in educational policy.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Critically evaluate the nativist account of language acquisition. In your answer: (1) explain the core claims of nativism, including the poverty of the stimulus argument; (2) consider the evidence for and against the existence of a Language Acquisition Device; and (3) explain how usage-based or social-pragmatic accounts offer an alternative. Aim for 200–250 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Chomsky's nativist account holds that children are born with a Language Acquisition Device — an innate, modular system containing Universal Grammar, the abstract principles common to all human languages. The poverty of the stimulus argument is the core empirical claim: children's linguistic input is too impoverished and inconsistent for complex grammatical rules to be learned through experience alone; therefore, some grammatical knowledge must be innate.

Supporting evidence includes: the universality of language development milestones across cultures; the existence of creolisation (pidgin languages developing into structurally complex creoles within a generation when children are exposed to them); and the critical period evidence, most dramatically demonstrated by Genie, who despite intensive teaching never acquired full syntactic competence after late childhood exposure. The creative, rule-governed nature of children's errors ('goed', 'feets') also suggests rule extraction beyond simple imitation.

Critics argue, however, that the poverty of the stimulus is exaggerated — statistical learning research (Saffran et al., 1996) shows that infants can extract complex distributional patterns from language input with remarkable efficiency, suggesting domain-general learning mechanisms may be more powerful than Chomsky assumed. Usage-based theories (Tomasello, 2003) propose that children learn language through the same cognitive tools used for other learning — intention-reading, joint attention, analogy, pattern recognition — without requiring language-specific modules. The success of large language models in acquiring grammatical competence from exposure to text (without any explicit grammar rules) suggests that the original poverty of the stimulus argument may have underestimated what can be learned from data.

The current consensus is likely interactionist: some language-specific predispositions, interacting with rich social input and domain-general learning mechanisms.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to your 16-year-old cousin why children saying 'goed' or 'mouses' is actually evidence of sophisticated mental processing, not just a mistake — and what this tells us about how language acquisition works.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Chomsky's argument that children's linguistic input is too limited and error-filled to explain their grammatical competence through learning alone, supporting the existence of innate grammatical knowledge.

The claim that full native-like language acquisition is possible only if exposure occurs during a developmental window (birth to puberty). After this period, language learning is possible but typically less complete.

The simplified, higher-pitched, clearly articulated speech register spontaneously used by caregivers when addressing infants (also called parentese or motherese). Supports phoneme discrimination and word segmentation.

The weak version of the hypothesis that the language we speak influences (but does not determine) how we think — particularly in domains where languages differ in their lexical categories or grammatical structures.

questions.questionHtml: What did Chomsky mean by the 'poverty of the stimulus' argument?
options: Children in poverty acquire language more slowly due to fewer words heard
Children's linguistic input is too impoverished and inconsistent to explain their grammatical competence through learning alone, suggesting innate grammatical knowledge
The language environment of most children lacks diversity of vocabulary
Language cannot be learned without explicit grammatical instruction
questions.correctAnswer: Children's linguistic input is too impoverished and inconsistent to explain their grammatical competence through learning alone, suggesting innate grammatical knowledge
questions.explanationHtml: Chomsky's 'poverty of the stimulus' (also called the 'poverty of the evidence') argument proposes that the speech children are exposed to is full of false starts, performance errors, and incomplete sentences — and is insufficient to explain the complex grammatical rules children nevertheless acquire rapidly, without formal instruction, and across all cultures. He used this to argue that children must be born with some innate grammatical knowledge (the Language Acquisition Device / Universal Grammar) that allows them to 'project' beyond their impoverished input.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: Hart and Risley's (1995) '30 million word gap' finding suggests that vocabulary development is primarily determined by genetic differences between children from different socioeconomic backgrounds.
questions.explanationHtml: False. Hart and Risley's finding is an environmental account — it demonstrates that children from different socioeconomic backgrounds hear dramatically different quantities and qualities of language, and that these differences predict later vocabulary and academic outcomes. The implication is that the vocabulary gap is caused primarily by differences in language environment (quantity of words heard, diversity of vocabulary, contingency of parent responses) rather than genetic differences. This finding is used to argue for early language intervention as a means of reducing educational inequality.

questions.questionHtml: Research shows that Russian speakers are faster than English speakers at discriminating between two shades of blue that cross the Russian lexical boundary (goluboy vs. siniy). This finding is best used as evidence for:
options: Strong linguistic determinism — you cannot perceive colours your language doesn't have words for
Weak linguistic relativity — the language we speak influences some aspects of perceptual cognition in specific domains
The universality of colour perception across all cultures and languages
The poverty of the stimulus — Russian children acquire colour terms faster due to richer input
questions.correctAnswer: Weak linguistic relativity — the language we speak influences some aspects of perceptual cognition in specific domains
questions.explanationHtml: This finding supports the weak version of the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (linguistic relativity): language-specific category boundaries influence the speed of perceptual discrimination — even a non-linguistic task (distinguishing blue shades) is affected by whether those shades fall within or across a lexical boundary. This is not strong linguistic determinism (English speakers can see all the same blue shades; they are just slightly slower to discriminate shades that don't cross an English category boundary). It does not support universality of colour perception (different languages produce different perceptual biases) or the poverty of the stimulus (which is about grammar, not colour terms).
